stem: In **hypertrophied hearts**, what did myocardial pH measurements show when **continuous antegrade cold blood cardioplegia** was compared with **intermittent cold cardioplegia**?

choices.text: The myocardial milieu was equally abnormal with both methods
The myocardial milieu became completely normal with continuous perfusion
The myocardial milieu was more normal, but not completely normal, with continuous perfusion
The myocardial milieu was more normal with intermittent cold cardioplegia
The myocardial milieu was more normal with continuous perfusion only when given retrograde

explanation.text: Myocardial pH data showed that, at least in **hypertrophied hearts**, the myocardial milieu is ==more normal, although not completely normal==, with continuous antegrade cold blood cardioplegia than with intermittent cold cardioplegia.

explanation.caption: Continuous cold cardioplegic perfusion
head: Route
What the chapter reports
rows: Alternative to single-dose and multidose intermittent cold cardioplegia; myocardial milieu more normal (not completely normal) in hypertrophied hearts
**Retrograde** continuous cold via the coronary sinus
Clinical experience: an excellent method of myocardial management; some give it after an initial antegrade cold dose
Retrograde cold blood after initial antegrade cold blood
_Experimentally_ found to maintain optimal myocardial pH

explanation.title: Better, not perfect
explanation.text: Continuous perfusion improved the milieu but did **not** make it completely normal.
the myocardial milieu is more normal, although not completely normal, with this method than with intermittent cold cardioplegia.
explanation.ref: Chapter 3: Myocardial Management During Cardiac Surgery with Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 99

choiceNotes.a: The milieu was **more normal** with continuous perfusion, not equally abnormal.
choiceNotes.b: The source stresses it was **not completely normal**.
choiceNotes.d: It is the **continuous** method that gave the more normal milieu.
choiceNotes.e: The pH finding concerns **antegrade** continuous cold blood cardioplegia; retrograde perfusion is described separately.

stem: A surgeon considers **continuous warm blood cardioplegia** for a CABG. Which statement best summarizes how the chapter assesses this technique?

choices.text: It gives good protection but is surgically inconvenient for certain operations
It is given without an initial antegrade dose, by the retrograde route only
It has been consistently superior to intermittent cold cardioplegia in all reports
It is limited to CABG and has not been used for other cardiac operations
It has been abandoned because its myocardial protection is poor

explanation.text: Continuous warm blood cardioplegia ==provides good myocardial protection==, but it is ==surgically inconvenient for certain operations==.

items: **Delivery**: antegrade or retrograde coronary sinus infusion **after an initial antegrade dose**.
**Use**: CABG **and other** cardiac operations.
**Evidence is mixed**: some found ventricular function recovery better than with intermittent cold cardioplegia; others found similar efficacy between warm and cold.

explanation.text: Although continuous warm blood cardioplegia provides good myocardial protection, it is surgically inconvenient for certain operations.
explanation.ref: Chapter 3: Myocardial Management During Cardiac Surgery with Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 100

choiceNotes.b: It is given antegrade **or** retrograde, and **after an initial antegrade dose**.
choiceNotes.c: Results are mixed: some groups found better recovery, others **similar efficacy** between warm and cold.
choiceNotes.d: It has been used for CABG **and other cardiac operations**.
choiceNotes.e: The source says it **provides good myocardial protection**.

stem: Which property does the chapter attribute to **cold cardioplegia with controlled aortic root reperfusion** (and warm cardioplegic induction when needed)?

choices.text: It markedly prolongs the operation compared with standard cardioplegia
It is frequently complicated by ventricular fibrillation during reperfusion
Its advantages have been clearly proven, so it is now used almost universally
It is best reserved for complex high-risk operations only
It is essentially devoid of ventricular fibrillation and minimizes stunning

explanation.text: The technique is ==essentially devoid of ventricular fibrillation==, ==minimizes myocardial stunning and necrosis==, is surgically convenient and prolongs the operation only mildly.

steps.text: Belief: control of **all aspects of reperfusion** may matter more than details of cold cardioplegia
During reperfusion the heart is **separated from events in the rest of the body** for a brief time

steps.label: claimed benefits
steps.text: Essentially no VF, less stunning and necrosis, apparently better postoperative cardiac performance

explanation.title: Not proven, not universal
items: Proof of its advantages has been **as difficult to obtain** as for other techniques, so it is **not yet widely used in its entirety**.
Using it only for high-risk cases brings the operational disadvantages of an **infrequently used** method, and even routine operations carry a small mortality and occasional morbidity.

explanation.title: Circuitry
explanation.text: A small **separate system** on the pump-oxygenator, with its own **miniaturized heat exchanger and two pumps**, delivers the solution at controlled temperature and pressure (aortic root, retrograde, or both).
The technique is surgically convenient, prolongs the operation only mildly, is essentially devoid of ventricular fibrillation, minimizes myocardial stunning and myocardial necrosis
explanation.ref: Chapter 3: Myocardial Management During Cardiac Surgery with Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 100

choiceNotes.a: It **prolongs the operation only mildly**.
choiceNotes.b: It is **essentially devoid** of ventricular fibrillation.
choiceNotes.c: Proof of its advantages has been difficult to obtain, and it is **not yet widely used** in its entirety.
choiceNotes.d: The chapter points out problems with restricting it to high-risk cases: an infrequently used method has operational disadvantages, and routine operations also carry risk.

stem: A child with a body surface area (BSA) of **0.75 m^2^** has an elective intracardiac repair under cardioplegia. With the aortic clamp still on, **warm terminal reperfusion ("hot shot")** with hyperkalemic, modified, enriched blood is given. After the initial low-pressure period, which **aortic root pressure target** and **total reperfusate volume** are used?

choices.text: 50 to 75 mmHg; 500 mL
50 to 75 mmHg; 250 mL
Normal systemic arterial diastolic pressure; 500 mL
Normal systemic arterial diastolic pressure; 250 mL
Normal systemic arterial systolic pressure; 375 mL

explanation.text: In infants and children with **BSA < 1 m^2^**, flow is increased until root pressure equals the ==normal systemic arterial diastolic pressure== (50 to 75 mmHg applies to adults). The 500-mL reperfusate is scaled when **BSA < 1.5 m^2^**: ==500 × BSA ÷ 1.5==, so 500 × 0.75 ÷ 1.5 = **250 mL**.

explanation.caption: Terminal warm reperfusion ("hot shot"), clamp on
head: Item
Adult
Infant/child
rows: Warm, hyperkalemic, modified, enriched blood cardioplegia
Root pressure after the initial low-pressure period

explanation.text: Two different BSA cut-offs: **< 1 m^2^** changes the pressure target; **< 1.5 m^2^** scales the volume. 375 mL is 500 × BSA without dividing by 1.5.
A total of 500 mL of the modified blood reperfusate is administered.
explanation.ref: Chapter 3: Myocardial Management During Cardiac Surgery with Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 100

choiceNotes.a: Both values are the **adult** ones; a child with BSA < 1 m^2^ is taken to normal diastolic pressure, and the volume is scaled.
choiceNotes.b: 50 to 75 mmHg is the **adult** target; below BSA 1 m^2^ the target is the normal systemic arterial diastolic pressure.
choiceNotes.c: The pressure is right, but for BSA < 1.5 m^2^ the volume is **500 × BSA ÷ 1.5** = 250 mL.
choiceNotes.e: The target is the **diastolic** pressure, and 375 mL omits the division by 1.5.

stem: After the warm terminal reperfusate ("hot shot") has been infused, controlled aortic root perfusion is continued with the **aortic clamp still in place**. Which perfusate is used, and what must the surgeon concentrate on during this phase?

choices.text: Normothermic, normokalemic, unmodified blood; avoiding ventricular distention
Warm, hyperkalemic, enriched blood; avoiding ventricular distention
Cold, hyperkalemic blood cardioplegia; avoiding myocardial rewarming
Normothermic, normokalemic, unmodified blood; keeping root pressure near 120 mmHg
Cold crystalloid cardioplegia; avoiding ventricular fibrillation

explanation.text: The circuit is switched to ==normothermic, normokalemic, unmodified blood==, and the surgeon must concentrate on ==avoiding ventricular distention==.

items: The heart stays **flaccid and electromechanically quiescent for 2 to 10 minutes** after the onset of controlled root reperfusion.
**Coronary resistance may rise** during this time → the perfusionist **reduces the flow rate** to keep a **constant aortic root pressure**.
The adverse effects of ventricular distention have been fully documented.

explanation.title: Two different reperfusates
explanation.text: Warm **hyperkalemic** modified blood is the initial 500-mL terminal reperfusate; what follows with the clamp on is **normokalemic, unmodified** blood.
During the controlled aortic root reperfusion, the surgeon must concentrate on avoiding ventricular distention
explanation.ref: Chapter 3: Myocardial Management During Cardiac Surgery with Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 100

choiceNotes.b: Warm hyperkalemic enriched blood is the **initial** terminal reperfusate; afterwards the perfusate is **normokalemic, unmodified** blood.
choiceNotes.c: Cold cardioplegia is not given during controlled reperfusion; the blood is **normothermic**.
choiceNotes.d: Root pressure must be kept from becoming excessively high (> 120 mmHg); 120 mmHg is not a target.
choiceNotes.e: Blood, not crystalloid, is used; and the surgeon's focus is **ventricular distention**.

stem: During controlled aortic root perfusion, cardiac action has resumed. Even the vented left ventricle ejects blood into the isolated aortic root, and the **aortic root pressure rises toward 130 mmHg**. What is the appropriate response?

choices.text: Release the aortic clamp immediately
Stop small-volume pulmonary ventilation
Increase the aortic root perfusion flow rate
Give a further dose of warm hyperkalemic reperfusate
Reduce the aortic root perfusion flow rate

explanation.text: The perfusionist must ==reduce the aortic root perfusion flow rate== to keep root pressure from becoming excessively high (**> 120 mmHg**), and at times places ==suction on the aortic root pressure catheter==.

steps.label: fix
steps.text: **Reduce root flow** ± suction on root pressure catheter

explanation.text: The perfusionist must be alert to the need to reduce the aortic root perfusion flow rate to keep the aortic root pressure from becoming excessively high
explanation.ref: Chapter 3: Myocardial Management During Cardiac Surgery with Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 100

choiceNotes.a: Controlled root perfusion continues until sinus rhythm and strong contractions return; the clamp is released later, after de-airing maneuvers.
choiceNotes.b: Small-volume ventilation is **begun** at this stage because the right ventricle pumps blood through the lungs.
choiceNotes.c: Increasing flow would raise root pressure further; flow must be **reduced**.
choiceNotes.d: The hyperkalemic reperfusate is the initial step; now the perfusate is normokalemic blood and the problem is excessive pressure.

stem: Controlled aortic root perfusion has been continued for a prolonged period, but **sinus rhythm with strong ventricular contractions cannot be achieved**. What does this indicate?

choices.text: This is expected; these endpoints usually take more than an hour
Imperfect myocardial management; post-CPB support almost certainly needed
The aortic clamp should be released and CPB discontinued at once
More warm hyperkalemic reperfusate should be infused to restore rhythm
The heart is simply hypothermic and will recover once rewarmed

explanation.text: If the endpoints cannot be reached, ==myocardial management was in some way imperfect==, and the patient ==almost certainly will require pharmacologic or mechanical support== after CPB.

head: Item
Detail
rows: Heart **flaccid and quiescent for 2 to 10 minutes**
Usual time from start of controlled reperfusion
Imperfect myocardial management → pharmacologic or mechanical support after CPB

explanation.text: When the endpoints cannot be reached, myocardial management was in some way imperfect, and the patient almost certainly will require pharmacologic or mechanical support after CPB.
explanation.ref: Chapter 3: Myocardial Management During Cardiac Surgery with Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 100

choiceNotes.a: The usual interval to reach the endpoints is **10 to 25 minutes**.
choiceNotes.c: Clamp release follows de-airing **after** the endpoints are reached; failure to reach them predicts the need for support.
choiceNotes.d: The chapter does not advise more hyperkalemic reperfusate; it interprets failure as imperfect myocardial management.
choiceNotes.e: The perfusate is normothermic blood; the chapter attributes failure to **imperfect myocardial management**.

stem: Sinus rhythm and strong contractions have returned during controlled aortic root perfusion. **Before the aortic clamp is released**, what does the perfusionist do?

choices.text: Continues root perfusion at 50 to 75 mmHg with the venous line fully open
Removes the root catheter and maximizes left ventricular vent suction
Gives a final dose of cold cardioplegia through the root catheter
Places strong suction on the root catheter and partly occludes the venous line
Fully opens the venous line so that the right ventricle stays empty

explanation.text: The perfusionist places ==strong suction (rather than perfusion) on the aortic root catheter== and ==partly occludes the venous line== so some blood passes through the right ventricle and lungs.

steps.text: **Strong suction** on aortic root catheter + **partial venous occlusion**

steps.label: anesthesiologist
steps.text: Intermittent **lung inflation** moves air from pulmonary veins and LA into the LV

steps.label: surgeon
steps.text: **Ballots** LA and pulmonary veins; LV ejects air into root → evacuated by suction

steps.label: then
steps.text: Blood volume rapidly augmented to **LA or PA wedge pressure 6–10 mmHg**

explanation.text: the perfusionist places strong suction (rather than perfusion) on the aortic root catheter and partly occludes the venous line so that some blood passes into the right ventricle and through the lungs
explanation.ref: Chapter 3: Myocardial Management During Cardiac Surgery with Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 100

choiceNotes.a: Root **perfusion** stops; strong **suction** is placed on the root catheter, and the venous line is **partly occluded**.
choiceNotes.b: The root catheter is used for **suction** to evacuate air during and after clamp release.
choiceNotes.c: At this stage the root catheter is used for **strong suction** to evacuate air, not for further cardioplegia.
choiceNotes.e: The venous line is **partly occluded** so that some blood passes through the right ventricle and lungs.

stem: A patient comes to operation in **acute cardiac failure with hemodynamic instability**. After median sternotomy, which myocardial management sequence is described for such an **energy-depleted heart**?

choices.text: CPB at 20°C, then cold induction followed by a 5-minute warm infusion
CPB at 35°C, then 2.5 minutes of antegrade and 2.5 minutes of retrograde cold infusion
CPB at 35°C, then cold cardioplegic induction alone, repeated every 20 minutes
CPB at 28°C, then a 3-minute warm infusion followed by 5 minutes of cold infusion
CPB at 35°C, then a 5-minute warm hyperkalemic infusion followed by 3 minutes of cold

explanation.text: CPB at ==35°C== is established quickly, the aorta is clamped, and ==warm hyperkalemic, modified, enriched blood ("warm induction") is given for 5 minutes==, then the same solution is made as cold as possible for ==another 3 minutes==.

explanation.title: Who has an energy-depleted heart?
items: Patients in **acute cardiac failure** with **hemodynamic instability**
Patients who are **severely cyanotic**

steps.text: CPB at **35°C**, as expeditiously as possible; aortic root catheter; aorta clamped

steps.label: 5 min
steps.text: **Warm induction** at the usual induction flow rate

steps.label: 3 min
steps.text: Same solution made **as cold as possible**

steps.label: every 20 min
steps.text: Cold infusions with potassium about **10 mmol/L**

explanation.text: Improving the **energy charge** of the heart **before** global myocardial ischemia probably results in better postoperative cardiac structure and function.
Patients who come to operation in acute cardiac failure with hemodynamic instability or are severely cyanotic have energy-depleted hearts.
explanation.ref: Chapter 3: Myocardial Management During Cardiac Surgery with Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 100

choiceNotes.a: CPB is established at **35°C**, and the **warm** infusion comes first (5 min), followed by cold.
choiceNotes.b: 2.5 min antegrade + 2.5 min retrograde is the **warm** induction used for acute LAD occlusion; here warm induction is 5 min, then 3 min cold.
choiceNotes.c: Energy-depleted hearts receive a 5-minute **warm induction** before the cold infusion.
choiceNotes.d: The durations are reversed (warm **5** min, then cold **3** min) and CPB is at **35°C**.

topic: Ancillary Measures for Preventing Myocardial Damage
stem: A patient undergoing CABG has been anesthetized, and **CPB has not yet started**. Which management principle helps prevent **important myocardial necrosis** during this pre-bypass period?

choices.text: Keeping ventricular end-diastolic pressures low
Keeping the heart rate moderately fast to support output
Keeping arterial pressure elevated to boost coronary flow
Keeping arterial oxygen tension low to limit oxygen demand
Keeping arterial pressure low to limit oxygen demand

explanation.text: Proper management ==avoids high ventricular end-diastolic pressures== (which harm **subendocardial perfusion**), avoids increased oxygen demand, and maintains oxygen supply. Important necrosis between induction and CPB occurs in **as many as 30% to 40%** of CABG patients when management is suboptimal, but can fall to **almost 3%** under optimal circumstances.

explanation.center: Proper management before and after CPB

children: Adequate cardiac output without deleterious effects

explanation.text: Patients other than CABG patients are also at risk, particularly those with **marked ventricular hypertrophy** or **reduced myocardial energy charge**.

explanation.title: After CPB too
explanation.text: Necrosis can also follow events **after CPB** that unbalance oxygen demand and supply: **catecholamines** used to treat low cardiac output early after CPB **can result in myocardial necrosis**.
It avoids high ventricular end-diastolic pressures and the concomitant detrimental effect on perfusion of the subendocardium.
explanation.ref: Chapter 3: Myocardial Management During Cardiac Surgery with Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 101

choiceNotes.b: **Tachycardia** increases myocardial oxygen demand and should be avoided.
choiceNotes.c: **Arterial hypertension** increases oxygen demand; good management maintains an adequate, not elevated, arterial pressure.
choiceNotes.d: Good management **maintains adequate arterial oxygen levels** to secure myocardial oxygen supply.
choiceNotes.e: Good management **maintains arterial blood pressure** to secure myocardial oxygen supply.

stem: Extensive **myocardial edema** is frequently seen after ischemia and reperfusion in animal studies. What did a careful **two-dimensional echocardiographic study in humans** show after uncomplicated cardiac operations using cardioplegia?

choices.text: A marked sudden increase in LV mass, as in the dog model
No increase in LV mass, unlike the dog model
A modest LV mass increase that resolved within days
Increased right but not left ventricular mass
No increase in humans or in the dog model

explanation.text: In humans, echocardiography ==failed to disclose any increase in LV mass== (a reasonably sensitive indicator of myocardial water), whereas ==the same study in a dog model showed a marked sudden increase==.

explanation.caption: Why animal inferences transfer with difficulty
head: Model
Problem
rows: Extensive edema after ischemia/reperfusion; **rarely evident clinically** (except prolonged severe damage and some operations in young patients)
Transferred with difficulty; worse if **crystalloid-perfused** (behaves differently from blood-perfused)
Age-defined immaturity in one species vs another is **uncertain**

explanation.text: Confirmation that animal-derived inferences apply to humans **must continually be sought**.
a careful study in humans using two-dimensional echocardiography failed to disclose any increase in left ventricular mass
explanation.ref: Chapter 3: Myocardial Management During Cardiac Surgery with Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 101

choiceNotes.a: The marked sudden increase was seen in the **dog**, not in humans.
choiceNotes.c: The human study found **no** increase in LV mass.
choiceNotes.d: The study assessed **left ventricular** mass and found no increase.
choiceNotes.e: The dog model **did** show a marked sudden increase.

stem: During cardiac surgery in a **neonate**, which measure does the chapter describe as being **of supreme importance** to optimize myocardial preservation?

choices.text: Overcoming the usually nonuniform coronary distribution of cardioplegia
Adding extra calcium to the cardioplegic solution
Giving frequent multidose cardioplegia
Preventing ventricular distension
Supplying fatty acids as the main energy substrate

explanation.text: The immature myocardium is limited in contractility and ==does not tolerate distension==; ==preventing ventricular distension== is of supreme importance.

children: Rarely any impediment to uniform cardioplegia delivery

explanation.text: Preventing ventricular distension during the course of neonatal cardiac surgery is of supreme importance to optimize myocardial preservation.
explanation.ref: Chapter 3: Myocardial Management During Cardiac Surgery with Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 101

choiceNotes.a: The immature myocardium **rarely** has impediments to uniform coronary (and cardioplegia) delivery.
choiceNotes.b: Pediatric solutions are often **hypocalcemic** to lower the risk of calcium overload.
choiceNotes.c: Multidose administration was shown **experimentally** to be disadvantageous in immature hearts.
choiceNotes.e: The neonatal heart preferentially uses **glucose**, not fatty acids.

stem: The **immature myocardium** can tolerate periods of hypoxia and ischemia while still generating adequate ATP. Which feature explains this?

choices.text: Preferential fatty acid oxidation and aerobic metabolism
Abundant cytosolic 5'-nucleotidase for regenerating ATP
A well-developed sarcoplasmic reticulum storing calcium
Strong expression of superoxide dismutase and catalase
Preferential glucose use with upregulated glycolytic enzymes

explanation.text: The neonatal heart ==preferentially uses glucose==, with ==upregulated glycolytic enzymes== (hexokinase, pyruvate kinase, phosphofructokinase), and has larger **amino acid stores** for anaerobic ATP production.

head: Feature
Adult heart
Immature heart
rows: **Larger**; anaerobic ATP via transamination and substrate-level phosphorylation of glutamate and pyruvate

explanation.text: This helps explain the demonstrated value of **amino acid supplementation** in improving tolerance of the immature heart to ischemia and hypoxia.
Some found the immature myocardium (< about **18 months**) **deficient** in cytosolic 5'-nucleotidase, so less able to convert cyclic AMP and inosine back to ATP.
the neonatal heart preferentially uses glucose as its energy substrate.
explanation.ref: Chapter 3: Myocardial Management During Cardiac Surgery with Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 101

choiceNotes.a: Fatty acid oxidation and aerobic metabolism are preferred by the **adult** heart.
choiceNotes.b: The immature myocardium has been found **deficient** in cytosolic 5'-nucleotidase.
choiceNotes.c: The immature sarcoplasmic reticulum is **incompletely developed**.
choiceNotes.d: Antioxidant enzymes are **less** well expressed in the immature cardiomyocyte.

stem: After neonatal cardiac surgery, **intravenous calcium** can be an effective inotropic agent, yet many pediatric cardioplegic solutions are **hypocalcemic** or contain magnesium. Which feature of the immature myocardium explains both?

choices.text: Immature sarcoplasmic reticulum with reliance on extracellular calcium
A sarcoplasmic reticulum that stores calcium better than in adults
Preferential use of glucose rather than fatty acid oxidation
Larger amino acid stores supporting anaerobic ATP production
Rapid angiogenesis balancing coronary supply and demand

explanation.text: The immature **sarcoplasmic reticulum** is incompletely developed with ==decreased SERCA== expression, so the cell is ==more dependent on extracellular calcium== for excitation-contraction coupling and is ==at risk of calcium overload==.

steps.label: consequence
steps.text: Poor intracellular calcium regulation and storage

branches.label: risk
branches.text: **Calcium overload** and injury after ischemia-reperfusion → hypocalcemic and/or magnesium-containing cardioplegia

explanation.text: Vulnerability is worsened by **incompletely developed antioxidant mechanisms** (superoxide dismutase, catalase, glutathione reductase less expressed).

the immature cardiomyocyte is less able to regulate intracellular calcium levels, cannot store calcium as effectively, and is, therefore, more dependent on extracellular calcium levels for EC coupling.
explanation.ref: Chapter 3: Myocardial Management During Cardiac Surgery with Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 102

choiceNotes.b: The immature SR is **incompletely developed** and stores calcium **less** effectively.
choiceNotes.c: Glucose preference explains ischemic tolerance, not calcium dependence.
choiceNotes.d: Amino acid stores support anaerobic ATP production, not calcium handling.
choiceNotes.e: Angiogenesis explains uniform coronary supply, not calcium handling.

stem: Normal immature hearts tolerate ischemia relatively well. For a **cyanotic neonate in heart failure** coming to open heart surgery, what does the chapter conclude about the heart's tolerance of global myocardial ischemia?

choices.text: It is greater than normal, because chronic hypoxia preconditions the heart
It equals that of a normal immature heart, since metabolism is unchanged
Probably not unusually high; failure and hypoxia cause postischemic depression
It is relevant only in chronic cyanosis; acute cyanosis has no effect
It is greater than normal, because cyanosis protects against atherosclerosis

explanation.text: Immature hearts ==in acute cardiac failure or recently subjected to hypoxia== develop ==profound functional depression== after ischemia that normal immature hearts tolerate; such patients probably have hearts ==not unusually resistant== to global ischemia.

items: Neonates and infants coming to surgery are **usually cyanotic, in heart failure, or both**, so they are unlikely to have normal myocardium.
Cyanosis, **acute and chronic**, accelerates ischemic damage and lessens postischemic recovery, probably through its effect on myocardial metabolism.

explanation.text: Chronic cyanosis seems to protect against **coronary atherosclerosis**; this does not make the heart resistant to ischemia, because cyanosis **lessens** postischemic recovery.
neonates and infants who come to open heart surgery probably have hearts that are not unusually resistant to the damaging effects of global myocardial ischemia.
explanation.ref: Chapter 3: Myocardial Management During Cardiac Surgery with Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 102

choiceNotes.a: Cyanosis **accelerates** ischemic damage and lessens postischemic recovery.
choiceNotes.b: Such hearts are unlikely to be normal; cyanosis probably acts through its **effect on myocardial metabolism**.
choiceNotes.d: Both **acute and chronic** cyanosis accelerate the damaging effects.
choiceNotes.e: Protection against coronary atherosclerosis does not translate into ischemic tolerance; cyanosis lessens postischemic recovery.

stem: Experimentally, **cyanotic neonates and infants** may suffer myocardial injury simply from **reoxygenation during the initial stages of CPB**. How may this hypoxemic/reoxygenation injury be avoided?

choices.text: By starting CPB with a hyperoxic prime to restore oxygenation quickly
By beginning CPB at the ambient oxygen tension of the hypoxemic patient
By delaying aortic cross-clamping until the patient is fully oxygenated
By using crystalloid instead of blood cardioplegia
By adding calcium to the CPB prime

explanation.text: Reoxygenation injury ==may be avoidable by beginning CPB at the ambient oxygen tension of the hypoxemic subject==.

steps.label: sudden reoxygenation on CPB
steps.text: ↑ Conjugated dienes, **hydroxyl radicals** → lipid peroxidation, nitric oxide release

explanation.title: Experimental adjuncts
explanation.text: Adding **deferoxamine** and antioxidants (such as catalase and coenzyme Q10) to the prime might limit oxidant damage; their importance in human neonates is **not yet clarified**.
This hypoxemic/reoxygenation injury may be avoidable by beginning CPB at the ambient oxygen tension of the hypoxemic subject.
explanation.ref: Chapter 3: Myocardial Management During Cardiac Surgery with Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 102

choiceNotes.a: Abrupt reoxygenation is the **cause** of the injury; CPB should begin at the patient's ambient oxygen tension.
choiceNotes.c: The injury arises from reoxygenation during the **initial stages of CPB**, not from cross-clamp timing.
choiceNotes.d: Reoxygenation injury is addressed through the oxygen tension at CPB start; one study even found cold **blood** cardioplegia superior to crystalloid St. Thomas solution in infants.
choiceNotes.e: The suggested prime additives are **deferoxamine and antioxidants**; the immature heart is at risk of calcium overload.

topic: Neonates and Infants: Methods of Myocardial Management
stem: In many neonatal operations, the procedure is done largely **through the right atrium**. Which view of neonatal myocardial management does the chapter put forward?

choices.text: Methods should differ fundamentally from those used in adults
Methods similar to adults, with retrograde blood cardioplegia
Crystalloid cardioplegia only, since blood is poorly tolerated
Multidose cardioplegia, proven superior in immature hearts
Antegrade root delivery only, as retrograde is not feasible

explanation.text: One point of view, compatible with all available evidence (though not with the opinions of some), is that the ==basic methodology in neonates, infants and children should be similar to that in adults==. With right atrial procedures, ==retrograde coronary sinus infusion of blood cardioplegia== should be particularly convenient.

items: Feasibility, safety and efficiency of **retrograde blood cardioplegia as maintenance** shown in the **arterial switch operation** and **complex arch reconstruction**.
One study: **cold blood** cardioplegia gave superior protection to **crystalloid St. Thomas** solution in infants and young children.
Experimentally, **multidose** administration was **disadvantageous** in immature hearts.
Little concerted effort has been made to overcome the **technical difficulty** in very small hearts.

explanation.text: Whatever the agent and protocol, all **catheters, cannulae, doses, flow rates and pressures** should be **scaled appropriately** to small patients.

the feasibility, safety, and efficiency of retrograde coronary sinus infusion of blood cardioplegic solution as maintenance cardioplegia have been demonstrated in the arterial switch operation and in complex arch reconstruction.
explanation.ref: Chapter 3: Myocardial Management During Cardiac Surgery with Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 102

choiceNotes.a: The view put forward is that methodology should be **similar** to that in adults.
choiceNotes.c: One study found **cold blood** cardioplegia superior to crystalloid St. Thomas solution in infants and young children.
choiceNotes.d: Multidose administration was shown **experimentally to be disadvantageous** in immature hearts.
choiceNotes.e: Retrograde blood cardioplegia has been shown **feasible and safe** in the arterial switch operation and complex arch reconstruction.

topic: Neonates and Infants: del Nido Cardioplegia
stem: **del Nido cardioplegic solution** is based on the extracellular composition of the Buckberg solutions. Which modification, with its rationale, is correct?

choices.text: Higher calcium, since pediatric myocardium relies on calcium flux
More magnesium, to further depress cell excitability during ischemia
Lidocaine added to depolarize the cell membrane and arrest the heart
Mannitol added as the principal arresting agent of the solution
Glutamate and aspartate added as the principal arresting agents

explanation.text: **Magnesium is increased** to ==depress cell excitability further== (and therefore cellular metabolism and ATP utilization) during the ischemic period. Calcium is **lower**, and **lidocaine** is added to block sodium channels.

explanation.caption: del Nido vs Buckberg base: major differences
head: Change
Reason
rows: Pediatric myocardium relies more on calcium flux for EC coupling and tolerates postischemic calcium overload poorly
Further depresses cell excitability (and metabolism, ATP use) during ischemia
Sodium channel block → less excitability, less calcium overload in early reperfusion

explanation.title: Table 3.1 roles
items: **Potassium chloride**: depolarizes the cell membrane
**Lidocaine**: maintains arrest in a hyperpolarized state
**Magnesium**: calcium channel blocker, prevents contractile activation
**Mannitol**: decreases edema, free radical scavenger

explanation.text: Magnesium is increased to depress cell excitability further (and therefore cellular metabolism and ATP utilization) during the ischemic period.
explanation.ref: Chapter 3: Myocardial Management During Cardiac Surgery with Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 102

choiceNotes.a: Calcium is **lower** in del Nido solution, because pediatric myocardium relies more on calcium flux and tolerates postischemic calcium overload poorly.
choiceNotes.c: **Potassium chloride** depolarizes the membrane; lidocaine is a sodium channel blocker that maintains arrest in a **hyperpolarized** state.
choiceNotes.d: Mannitol decreases myocardial edema and scavenges free radicals; potassium, lidocaine and magnesium are the arresting agents.
choiceNotes.e: Glutamate and aspartate are discussed for warm induction and reperfusate in experimental studies, not as del Nido arresting agents.

topic: Neonates and Infants: del Nido Cardioplegia
stem: Which statement summarizes the accumulated **clinical experience with del Nido cardioplegia** in neonates, infants and children, compared with **Buckberg cardioplegia**?

choices.text: Slower return of sinus rhythm, but fewer doses needed
Clearly superior to HTK solution in every randomized trial
Longer cross-clamp times because of more frequent redosing
Now rarely used; most centers have returned to Buckberg
Faster return of sinus rhythm despite longer dosing intervals

explanation.text: Experience has been very favorable: most surgeons note ==more rapid return of sinus rhythm== and excellent cardiac function ==despite longer recommended intervals between doses== (up to 90 min vs 20–30 min with Buckberg).

head: Item
del Nido
rows: **20 cc/kg**; up to **30 cc/kg** additional for hypertrophied hearts (center dependent)
Randomized trials vs HTK, Custodiol, St. Thomas
Some: no significant clinical difference; others: improved markers of myocardial injury
Most commonly used formulation (**38%** of responses)

explanation.text: most surgeons noting more rapid return of sinus rhythm and excellent cardiac function despite longer recommended periods between cardioplegia administration (up to 90 min vs. 20-30 min) compared with Buckberg cardioplegia.
explanation.ref: Chapter 3: Myocardial Management During Cardiac Surgery with Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 102

choiceNotes.a: Most surgeons note **more rapid** return of sinus rhythm.
choiceNotes.b: Some trials showed **no significant clinical difference**; others showed improved markers of myocardial injury.
choiceNotes.c: Most studies showed **decreased** cross-clamp times and **fewer** doses.
choiceNotes.d: A Congenital Heart Surgeons' Society survey found del Nido the **most commonly used** formulation (38%).

stem: A patient with **severe aortic stenosis** and marked left ventricular hypertrophy undergoes aortic valve replacement. What is the **single most important change** in myocardial management?

choices.text: Increasing the amount of cardioplegia given
Using retrograde cardioplegia as the only route
Using crystalloid instead of blood cardioplegia
Lengthening the interval between reinfusions to 60 minutes
Lowering the cardioplegic flow to protect the subendocardium

explanation.text: Because of high heart weight and severe hypertrophy with difficult subendocardial perfusion, the single most important change is to ==increase the amount of cardioplegia given==.

items: Blood cardioplegia **> 300 mL/min for 5 min**.
**Antegrade and retrograde** delivery.
Reinfusion **after 20 minutes**, also at higher volumes (**250–300 mL/min**).

explanation.text: **Any incomplete delivery** of cardioplegia must be avoided and will result in myocardial damage.
Myocardial management must be adapted to this special situation with a significantly higher heart weight, severe hypertrophy, and, consequently, difficult perfusion of the subendocardial layer.
explanation.ref: Chapter 3: Myocardial Management During Cardiac Surgery with Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 103

choiceNotes.b: The example uses **antegrade and retrograde** delivery.
choiceNotes.c: The example given is **blood** cardioplegia at higher volumes.
choiceNotes.d: Reinfusion is given **after 20 minutes**.
choiceNotes.e: Flow is **increased** (> 300 mL/min) because subendocardial perfusion is difficult.

source.ref: Chapter 3: Myocardial Management During Cardiac Surgery with Cardiopulmonary Bypass

stem: A patient needing aortic valve replacement has **mild aortic regurgitation**. Initial cardioplegia is infused antegrade through the unopened aortic root, and **root pressure stays adequate**, confirming minimal runoff. What is done next?

choices.text: Aortotomy at once, with infusion switched to the coronary ostia
LA vent suction increased and the infusion stopped
LA vent clamped, infusion continued, LV gently massaged
Infusion switched to the retrograde route only
Aortic clamp released briefly to decompress the LV

explanation.text: With adequate root pressure, the ==left atrial vent line is clamped==, the infusion continues, and the ==left ventricle is gently massaged== manually; this prevents LV distention and helps perfuse the coronary arteries.

explanation.title: Mild AR: initial antegrade infusion via unopened root

branches.label: adequate (minimal runoff)
branches.text: Clamp LA vent, continue infusion, **gently massage LV**

explanation.text: Unless the aortic valve is completely competent (uncommon), induction for aortic valve repair or replacement is best by **direct ostial infusion preceded by retrograde induction** via the coronary sinus.
the left atrial vent line is clamped, the infusion continues, and the left ventricle is gently massaged manually during the infusion period.
explanation.ref: Chapter 3: Myocardial Management During Cardiac Surgery with Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 103

choiceNotes.a: An aortotomy with direct ostial infusion is for **excessive runoff**; here runoff is minimal.
choiceNotes.b: The LA vent line is **clamped** and the infusion **continues**.
choiceNotes.d: With adequate root pressure the antegrade infusion simply **continues**.
choiceNotes.e: Distention is prevented by **manual LV massage**, not clamp release.

stem: During aortic valve surgery, after brief electrical fibrillation the aorta is clamped and antegrade cardioplegia is started, but **aortic root pressure is below 50 mmHg**. In the sequence described, what follows?

choices.text: Increase antegrade root flow until root pressure exceeds 100 mmHg
Start retrograde delivery and open the aorta for ostial cannulae
Stop all cardioplegia and cool the patient systemically to 20°C
Continue antegrade root infusion and massage the left ventricle
Release the aortic clamp and repeat induction after defibrillation

explanation.text: If root pressure is ==< 50 mmHg==, ==retrograde cardioplegia is started (at > 300 mL/min)== and the proximal aorta is opened with a **hockey-stick incision** for coronary ostial cannulae.

steps.text: Brief electrical VF → aortic clamp → antegrade cardioplegia

steps.label: ostial cannulae
steps.text: Left 2 min then right 2 min, **or** both simultaneously; retrograde stopped once antegrade established

steps.label: maintenance
steps.text: Reinfusions every **20–25 min** (retrograde, antegrade or simultaneous)

explanation.title: Cross-clamp > 90 min
items: Add **antegrade ostial** delivery at **every third** reinfusion, besides retrograde application every 20–30 min.
The warm terminal reperfusion ("hot shot") can be given antegrade via the **aortic root cannula** once the valve is repaired or replaced.

explanation.text: Direct cannulation of the ostia (especially **multiple cannulation maneuvers**) may lead to **later ostial stenosis**.
Once antegrade cardioplegic perfusion has been established, retrograde delivery is stopped.
explanation.ref: Chapter 3: Myocardial Management During Cardiac Surgery with Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 103

choiceNotes.a: Low root pressure here prompts **retrograde** delivery (> 300 mL/min) and direct ostial cannulation, not higher root flow.
choiceNotes.c: Systemic cooling to 20°C is the response to large noncoronary collateral flow, not to low root pressure in valve surgery.
choiceNotes.d: Continuing root infusion with LV massage is for mild AR with **adequate** root pressure.
choiceNotes.e: The described sequence continues with retrograde and ostial delivery; the clamp is not released.

stem: During a cardiac operation in a patient with **aortic regurgitation too mild to justify valve replacement**, an appropriate aortic root pressure could not be achieved, so cold cardioplegia was given **retrogradely through the coronary sinus**. How is the **reperfusion phase** managed?

choices.text: Warm hyperkalemic, then normokalemic, all retrograde
Warm hyperkalemic via the aortic root at higher flow
No controlled reperfusion; the clamp is released
Normokalemic only, through direct ostial cannulae
Cold retrograde, then warm via the aortic root

explanation.text: The heart can be carried through the ==initially warm hyperkalemic reperfusion and then the normokalemic reperfusion== until cardiac action fully resumes, using ==exclusively retrograde perfusion through the coronary sinus==.

branches.label: root pressure not achievable
branches.text: **Retrograde** cold cardioplegia + **retrograde** reperfusion (warm hyperkalemic → normokalemic) until cardiac action fully resumes

explanation.text: In the reperfusion phase, the heart can be carried through the initially warm hyperkalemic reperfusion and then the normokalemic reperfusion until cardiac action fully resumes, using exclusively retrograde perfusion through the coronary sinus.
explanation.ref: Chapter 3: Myocardial Management During Cardiac Surgery with Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 104

choiceNotes.b: The root cannot hold an appropriate pressure; reperfusion is **exclusively retrograde**.
choiceNotes.c: Controlled reperfusion is still performed, **retrogradely**, until cardiac action fully resumes.
choiceNotes.d: The aorta is not opened; the usual warm hyperkalemic then normokalemic sequence is given **retrograde**.
choiceNotes.e: Reperfusion is **warm** (hyperkalemic, then normokalemic) and **exclusively retrograde**.

source.ref: Chapter 3: Myocardial Management During Cardiac Surgery with Cardiopulmonary Bypass

stem: A patient in **cardiogenic shock** is brought to the operating room shortly after **acute LAD occlusion**. Which element belongs to the myocardial management program described?

choices.text: 20 minutes of controlled regional reperfusion of the LAD
Warm induction given antegrade only, for 5 minutes
An ITA graft to the LAD instead of any vein graft
A single cold cardioplegic dose with no further infusions
Clamp release right after the last distal anastomosis

explanation.text: The program includes ==prolonged (20 min) controlled regional reperfusion== of the LAD (or culprit vessel) with ==hyperkalemic modified blood==.

items: Initial controlled **warm** cardioplegia: **2.5 min antegrade + 2.5 min retrograde** (coronary sinus).
At least a **vein graft** to the LAD (or the culprit vessel).
**20 min** controlled **regional reperfusion** of the culprit artery with hyperkalemic modified blood.

explanation.text: Initial warm cardioplegia followed by usual cold cardioplegia produces quiescence; during grafting, intermittent cold infusions continue, **antegrade and retrograde alternately** or as dictated by ease of delivery or number of grafts.
Prolonged (20 min) controlled regional reperfusion with hyperkalemic modified blood of the LAD
explanation.ref: Chapter 3: Myocardial Management During Cardiac Surgery with Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 104

choiceNotes.b: Warm induction is **2.5 min antegrade and 2.5 min retrograde**; 5 min antegrade is the energy-depleted heart protocol.
choiceNotes.c: The program calls for **at least a vein graft** to the LAD.
choiceNotes.d: Cold cardioplegia is supplemented by **additional intermittent infusions** during grafting.
choiceNotes.e: The program includes **20 min** of controlled regional reperfusion of the culprit vessel.

stem: During CABG in a patient with long-standing severe coronary disease, the arrested heart **begins to show electromechanical activity** despite venting and multidose cardioplegia, from **large noncoronary collateral flow** washing out the cardioplegia. What is recommended?

choices.text: Increase CPB flow and give continuous warm cardioplegia
Release the clamp and complete the grafts on the beating heart
Systemic cooling to 20°C, lower CPB flow, more cold cardioplegia
Increase left ventricular vent suction and continue as usual
Give only retrograde cardioplegia at normothermia

explanation.text: At the first sign, the perfusate is made ==as cold as possible until the patient reaches 20°C==, CPB flow is reduced to ==about 1 L/min/m^2^==, and ==another dose of cold cardioplegia== is given.

steps.label: response
steps.text: Cool to **20°C** → perfusate 20°C, flow **about 1 L/min/m^2^** → repeat **cold cardioplegia**

explanation.text: Another dose of cold cardioplegia is then administered.
explanation.ref: Chapter 3: Myocardial Management During Cardiac Surgery with Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 104

choiceNotes.a: CPB flow is **reduced** (about 1 L/min/m^2^), and **cold**, not warm, cardioplegia is given.
choiceNotes.b: The chapter keeps the heart arrested with cooling, low flow and more cold cardioplegia.
choiceNotes.d: Activity restarts **despite** venting; cooling and low flow are needed.
choiceNotes.e: The response is systemic cooling to **20°C** with another **cold** dose.

source.ref: Chapter 3: Myocardial Management During Cardiac Surgery with Cardiopulmonary Bypass

stem: A critically ill patient with **active rheumatic pericarditis** needs **multiple-valve surgery** for aortic and mitral regurgitation. If **cold cardioplegia** is used, what else is necessary?

choices.text: Continuous warm cardioplegia instead of intermittent doses
Low-flow hypothermic perfusion and repeated cardioplegic infusions
A single cardioplegic dose without any reinfusion
Full-flow normothermic perfusion throughout bypass
Retrograde delivery only, avoiding any root infusion

explanation.text: The extensive, ==vascular pericardial adhesions==, if divided, cause excessive bleeding and ==excessive collateral coronary flow==; with cold cardioplegia, ==low-flow hypothermic perfusion and repeated cardioplegic infusions== are necessary.
If cold cardioplegia is used, low-flow hypothermic perfusion and repeated cardioplegic infusions are necessary.
explanation.ref: Chapter 3: Myocardial Management During Cardiac Surgery with Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 104

choiceNotes.a: The source specifies **cold** cardioplegia with low-flow **hypothermic** perfusion.
choiceNotes.c: **Repeated** cardioplegic infusions are necessary, because divided vascular adhesions add collateral coronary flow.
choiceNotes.d: Perfusion should be **low-flow** and **hypothermic**.
choiceNotes.e: The source does not restrict the route here; it requires low-flow hypothermic perfusion and repeated infusions.

stem: At **reoperative CABG**, a **patent internal thoracic artery (ITA) graft** is present. In most cases, how is it managed during the cardioplegic period, and what is the alternative?

choices.text: Left open routinely, with normothermic CPB and continuous warm cardioplegia
Ligated and divided permanently, with cardioplegia given only retrograde
Left open routinely, with antegrade root cardioplegia alone at 32°C
Partially mobilized and occluded; or left open, with CPB at 20–25°C
Fully mobilized and transposed before any cardioplegia is given

explanation.text: In most cases a patent ITA graft is ==identified by careful dissection, partially mobilized and occluded== during the cardioplegic period. Alternatively, it is ==left open with CPB at 20°C to 25°C==, frequent cardioplegia and **intermittent fibrillation**.
In most cases, a patent internal thoracic artery graft should be identified by careful dissection, partially mobilized, and occluded during the cardioplegic period.
explanation.ref: Chapter 3: Myocardial Management During Cardiac Surgery with Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 104

choiceNotes.a: If left open, CPB is conducted at **20–25°C** with frequent cardioplegia and intermittent fibrillation.
choiceNotes.b: The ITA is **occluded** temporarily during the cardioplegic period, not divided; antegrade and retrograde infusions are complementary.
choiceNotes.c: If left open, CPB is at **20–25°C** with frequent cardioplegia and intermittent fibrillation.
choiceNotes.e: It is only **partially** mobilized and occluded.

source.ref: Chapter 3: Myocardial Management During Cardiac Surgery with Cardiopulmonary Bypass

stem: During **reoperative cardiac surgery**, more frequent cardioplegic infusions and/or a lower systemic perfusion temperature are advised. What is the reason given?

choices.text: Patent vein grafts block antegrade delivery
The coronary sinus cannot be cannulated
Reoperative hearts are severely hypertrophied
Patent ITA grafts must be left open
Adhesions make the myocardium rewarm faster

explanation.text: ==Because of adhesions, the myocardium tends to rewarm more quickly than usual==, so more frequent cardioplegia, low systemic perfusion temperature, or both are appropriate.

items: Establish cardioplegic protection **early**, usually **before mobilization** of the cardiac mass.
Antegrade and retrograde infusions are **complementary**: place the retrograde catheter accurately (minimal sharp dissection over the **acute margin of the RV**, then posterior freeing dissection).
With **saphenous vein grafts left in place**, aortic root antegrade plus retrograde infusion seems the surest way to near-optimal delivery at induction.

explanation.text: Because of adhesions, the myocardium tends to rewarm more quickly than usual.
explanation.ref: Chapter 3: Myocardial Management During Cardiac Surgery with Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 104

choiceNotes.a: With vein grafts in place, **antegrade root plus retrograde** infusion is the surest delivery; the stated reason for frequent dosing is faster rewarming.
choiceNotes.b: The retrograde catheter **can** be placed accurately via dissection over the acute margin of the RV.
choiceNotes.c: Hypertrophy is not the stated reason; **adhesions** cause faster rewarming.
choiceNotes.d: A patent ITA is usually **occluded**; leaving it open is only an alternative.
